37324: The sick call the community's elders to pray and anoint with oil, combining Jewish practices of prayer and healing with communal confession.
37325:
James is the most clearly Jewish letter in the New Testament and could almost be read in a synagogue. It addresses believers as 'the twelve tribes', the scattered people of Israel whom God would one day regather. It calls the Torah 'the perfect law of liberty' and 'the royal law', summed up in Leviticus 19:18, 'love your neighbour as yourself'. Its heroes are Abraham, Rahab, Job and Elijah. Its central concern is the Jewish ideal of wholeness: a single-minded heart toward God rather than a 'double-minded' one, echoing the Shema's call to love God with all one's heart.

For James, faith (pistis) is trust and loyalty toward the God who is one, and like any covenant loyalty it must be lived out. Abraham's trust was 'completed' when he offered Isaac; Rahab's showed itself in sheltering the spies. This is how a first-century Jewish audience understood covenant faithfulness: God's gracious gift, 'every good and perfect gift from above', calls forth a response of mercy, justice and humility. Jesus appears as 'the Lord of glory' whose coming is near, and the ethics of his kingdom shape the whole letter, which stands as a living link between Jesus' teaching and the earliest Jewish believers.
37327: Testing produces endurance and maturity; ask God for wisdom without doubting.
37329: Receive the implanted word and do it; true religion cares for orphans and widows.
37331: Honouring the rich and shaming the poor breaks the royal law of love.
37333: Faith without deeds is dead; Abraham and Rahab show living trust.
37335: Speech can set a forest on fire; heavenly wisdom is peaceable and merciful.
37337: Quarrels come from desires; submit to God, do not judge, do not boast about tomorrow.
37339: Woe to oppressive rich; wait for the Lord, pray, confess and restore the wandering.
37362: Mature, undivided, whole-hearted; the goal of trials and the quality of God's law.
37364: Literally 'two-souled': divided loyalty between God and the world.
37366: Trust and allegiance to God that is shown in action.
37368: To declare or demonstrate as righteous; in James, Abraham is shown righteous by his actions.
37369: Many sayings echo the Sermon on the Mount: trials, mercy, oaths, the poor and doing the word.
37370: Leviticus 19, the holiness code, underlies James' teaching on love, partiality, wages and speech.
37371: Wisdom, speech and humility echo Proverbs; James quotes it on God's grace to the humble.
37372: Both cite Abraham and Genesis 15:6, but James focuses on faith shown in deeds, Paul on works of the Law as identity markers.
37373: James the leader appears in Acts guiding the council and receiving Paul.
37374: James rarely names Jesus but is saturated with his teaching. He calls him 'our glorious Lord Jesus Christ' and awaits his coming as Judge. Jewish readers often find James familiar, a Torah-centred ethical work; Christians read it as showing what trust in Jesus looks like in daily life, especially toward the poor.
37375: James contradicts Paul on faith and works
37376: Many readers feel James 2:24 ('a person is justified by works and not by faith alone') contradicts Paul's 'justified by faith apart from works of the law', and either downplay James, as Luther did, or explain it away.
37377: James Dunn and others note that Paul's 'works of the law' focus on Torah markers such as circumcision and food laws that divided Jews from Gentiles, while James' 'works' are acts of mercy, like clothing the poor. James' 'faith' in 2:19 is bare belief that God is one, which even demons have. Matthew Bates argues both writers see pistis as loyal trust that is embodied. On this reading they address different problems with compatible answers.
37378: Reformed scholars such as Douglas Moo and Thomas Schreiner agree there is no contradiction but explain it differently: Paul speaks of the initial verdict of justification by faith alone, and James of the evidence that faith is genuine (faith alone saves, but the faith that saves is never alone). Some critical scholars think James is reacting to a misunderstanding of Paul. All agree the tension is apparent, not a real clash over essentials.
37379: Hearing James on his own terms prevents a Christianity that claims faith but ignores the poor, and helps readers see Paul and James as partners.
37380: James told scattered, often poor Jewish believers that their faith in the Lord Jesus meant living out Torah's heart: patience under trial, justice for workers, honour for the poor and peace in the community.
37381: James confronts favouritism toward the wealthy, careless or cruel speech and faith that never touches the poor. It calls churches to prayer, confession and practical mercy.
37382: A letter to Gentile converts in Asia Minor telling them that, though now outsiders in their own towns, they have become God's own people, Israel's 'royal priesthood', called to hope and do good under suffering.
37384: Simon Peter, the Galilean fisherman who led the Twelve, writing late in life from Rome, with Silvanus (Silas) helping to write or deliver the letter.
37385: The letter claims Peter as author and was widely accepted early; 2 Peter refers to it and Polycarp echoes it. Many critical scholars doubt Petrine authorship because of its polished Greek and a setting they date later, while others point to Silvanus' role and to the absence of any clear evidence of later empire-wide persecution.
37388: Jewish writers after 70 (for example 4 Ezra and 2 Baruch) and Revelation call Rome 'Babylon', the empire that destroyed the temple and scattered God's people.
37389: 'Elect exiles of the dispersion' in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, mostly Gentile converts
37390: Northern and central Asia Minor (modern Turkey)
37391: Former pagans had stopped taking part in family cults, guild feasts and civic festivals. Neighbours were surprised and offended, slandering them as wrongdoers. This was mainly local social hostility, not yet an empire-wide legal persecution.
37393: Fire of Rome; Christians executed by Nero.
37394: Peter's martyrdom in Rome according to tradition (c. 64-68).
37395: Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia-Pontus, writes to Trajan about how to handle Christians.
37396:
The provinces named in the opening verse cover a vast area of what is now Turkey, from the Black Sea coast to the central plateau. Most of the believers there were Gentiles: Peter speaks of 'the futile ways inherited from your forefathers' and says that 'once you were not a people'. When they turned to Israel's God, they also turned away from household gods, trade-guild banquets dedicated to patron deities and festivals honouring the emperor, all of which bound ancient communities together.

The result was social exclusion. Neighbours were 'surprised that you do not join them' and spoke evil of them. Slaves in pagan households and wives of unbelieving husbands were especially exposed, since they were expected to follow the religion of the head of the house. John Elliott argued that many readers may already have been literal resident aliens (paroikoi), people without full civic rights; others think Peter's 'exile' language is mainly spiritual. Either way, they felt like strangers at home.

Around fifty years later, Pliny, governor of Bithynia, wrote that he executed people simply for being Christians if they refused to recant. 1 Peter shows an earlier stage in which the name 'Christian' was already a reason for shame.
37397: Slander was a weapon to shame outsiders into conformity. Peter reverses the values: suffering as a Christian is no shame but glorifies God, and God gives honour to those who trust the rejected cornerstone.
37399: Greek moralists taught how slaves, wives and husbands should behave in a well-ordered household. Peter adapts the form, addressing slaves and wives as moral agents and grounding everything in Christ's example, so that good conduct may silence slander and win others.
37401: Paroikoi and parepidemoi were people living away from home without full rights. The terms recall Abraham, a sojourner in Canaan, and Israel in exile.
37403: Peter says 'fear God, honour the emperor': the emperor is honoured as a human institution, but fear (reverence) is reserved for God alone, a quiet refusal of emperor worship.
37404: The dispersion was the Jewish experience of living scattered among the nations. Peter applies it to Gentile believers who now share Israel's identity and longing.
37405:
1 Peter does something remarkable: it addresses mainly Gentile converts with the titles of Israel. They are 'elect exiles of the dispersion', 'a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession', the very words God spoke to Israel at Sinai. 'Once you were not a people, but now you are God's people', Peter says, applying Hosea's promise of Israel's restoration. They are called to 'be holy, for I am holy', the refrain of Leviticus.

For a Jewish-rooted reader this is not Israel being replaced but Gentiles being brought into Israel's story, as the prophets foresaw the nations joining Israel's God. Their experience of marginalisation now matches Israel's long experience of exile under empires, which is why Rome is called 'Babylon'. Christ is presented through Isaiah's suffering servant, who bore sins and did not retaliate, and as the stone rejected by the builders in Psalm 118. The letter's hope is resurrection and 'an inheritance imperishable, kept in heaven' to be revealed at the last time, the Jewish hope of a renewed creation, not escape from it.
37407: Through Jesus' resurrection believers have a sure inheritance, and trials refine their faith like gold.
37409: Redeemed by Christ's blood, they are to live as holy people and love one another earnestly.
37411: Living stones in God's temple, a royal priesthood, they live honourably among the nations.
37413: Citizens, slaves, wives and husbands follow Christ's pattern of non-retaliation and good conduct.
37415: Ready to give a reason for hope, they share the path of Christ who suffered and was vindicated.
37417: Elders shepherd willingly; all resist the devil, trusting God who will restore them.
37418: Hope for God's people in exile
37439: Resident alien or temporary resident, living without full belonging.
37441: Confident expectation grounded in Jesus' resurrection.
37442: God's generous favour and gift, which calls for a relationship of trust; 'the true grace of God' in which to stand.
37444: Honourable way of life visible to outsiders.
37445: Israel's Sinai calling as a kingdom of priests is applied to believers.
37446: Isaiah 53 shapes the picture of Christ suffering without retaliation, and Isaiah 28 the cornerstone.
37447: 'Not my people' becoming 'my people' describes Gentile inclusion.
37448: Peter names 'Mark my son' with him in Babylon, linking him to the Gospel tradition.
37449: Both call Rome 'Babylon' and encourage faithful witness under pressure.
37450: Christ is the suffering servant who bore sins on the tree, the precious cornerstone, the shepherd and overseer of souls, and the one raised and exalted over all powers. Jewish readers recognise the use of Isaiah 53 and the transfer of Israel's titles; Christians read it as Gentiles joining Israel's priestly calling through the Messiah.
37451: 'Exiles' means this world is not our home, so we are just passing through to heaven
37452: Pilgrim and exile language is often read as saying the earth does not matter and believers should look past it to heaven.
37453: Exile in Jewish thought meant living faithfully among the nations while awaiting God's restoration, as Jeremiah told exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon. Peter calls believers to good works that outsiders can see, and their hope is an inheritance to be revealed when Christ appears. John Elliott, Karen Jobes and David deSilva read the language socially: they are outsiders in their towns but insiders in God's household.
37454: Evangelical scholars agree that the letter's hope is future and heavenly in source but emphasise that it is meant to shape present life, not to escape it. Jobes argues that literal displacement may also be in view. There is broad agreement that withdrawal from the world is not Peter's point.
37455: Seeing exile as faithful presence calls believers to do good where they live rather than retreat.
37456: The household code makes submission of slaves and wives a timeless rule
37457: Some read 1 Peter 2-3 as God's permanent blueprint for social order, including male authority and acceptance of harsh treatment; others reject the letter as endorsing slavery.
37458: David Balch and others showed Peter is using a familiar Greco-Roman form to show that believers are not subversive troublemakers, so that slander would be silenced and outsiders might be won. Remarkably, Peter addresses slaves and wives directly as moral agents, tells husbands to honour wives as co-heirs, and frames everything with Christ's example. It is a missional strategy for a vulnerable minority.
37459: Complementarian scholars (for example Wayne Grudem and Thomas Schreiner) see a lasting pattern of husbands' loving leadership grounded beyond culture, while acknowledging slavery is not endorsed; egalitarian scholars (for example Lynn Cohick and Craig Keener) see the code as cultural accommodation for mission. This is a live scholarly debate.
37460: These verses have been used to tell abused people to stay silent. Reading them in context shows Peter's concern for the vulnerable and for witness, not for enforcing abuse.
37461: For converts who had lost status and friendships, Peter gave a new family, a noble identity drawn from Israel's story, and a strategy of patient goodness under pressure.
37462: 1 Peter helps believers who feel culturally sidelined to keep hope, answer with gentleness, do visible good and find belonging in a community, without retreat or retaliation.
37463: A farewell testament in Peter's name, reminding believers to grow in godliness, trust the apostolic witness and the prophets, and not be shaken by those who mock the Lord's delayed coming.
37465: The letter presents itself as the last words of 'Simeon Peter', using the Hebrew form of his name, who knows his death is near and who was an eyewitness of the transfiguration.
37466: The text names Peter, but it is the New Testament letter most widely judged pseudonymous: its elaborate Greek differs from 1 Peter, chapter 2 closely reuses Jude, it refers to Paul's letters as a collection alongside 'the other Scriptures', and it treats the first generation as having died. It is first named explicitly by Origen (third century), who notes it was disputed. Defenders such as Michael Green and Michael Kruger answer that a different secretary could explain the style, that Peter could have used Jude, and that the early church rejected other Petrine writings, so its acceptance was not careless. Some scholars, such as Richard Bauckham, see it as a 'testament' whose readers would have recognised the convention of writing in an honoured figure's name.
37468: Rome, if by Peter; otherwise unknown
37469: Tradition places Peter's death in Rome under Nero; nothing in the letter names a place.
37470: Believers who had received 'a faith of equal standing', apparently the same readers as an earlier letter
37471: Possibly the churches of Asia Minor addressed in 1 Peter
37472: Teachers inside the community were promising freedom while living in sensuality and greed, and scoffers asked 'where is the promise of his coming?', arguing that the world simply goes on as it always has.
37473: Nero's persecution; tradition dates Peter's martyrdom to 64-68.
37474: Destruction of Jerusalem; the first generation of apostles is passing away.
37476: Origen mentions 2 Peter as a disputed writing (approximate).
37477: Athanasius' Festal Letter lists 2 Peter among the 27 New Testament books.
37478:
2 Peter is written as a 'testament', a well-known Jewish genre in which a great figure near death gives final instructions and warnings, as Moses does in Deuteronomy and as the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs portray Jacob's sons doing. Peter says the 'putting off of my tent' is near and that he wants his readers to remember these things after his departure.

The problem it addresses is twofold. Some teachers were living immorally and greedily while claiming freedom, and they mocked the expectation of Christ's return. Jerome Neyrey and others have compared their arguments with Epicurean philosophy, which denied that the gods intervene in the world or judge it: if the world never changes, there will be no judgment, so there is no need for moral restraint. The author answers that God has acted in judgment before (the flood, Sodom), that his timing is not ours ('one day is as a thousand years'), and that the delay is mercy, giving time for repentance.

The letter's acceptance into the canon was slow. Eusebius lists it among the disputed books, and some early writers doubted it. It was received in the fourth-century lists that settled the 27-book New Testament.
37480: Jewish farewell speeches recall the past, warn of coming false teachers and urge faithfulness. The form was widely known and often written in a hero's name.
37482: Greek moralists listed virtues building on one another. Peter's 'ladder' starts with faith and ends with love, rooting Greek moral language in God's gift.
37484: God's 'divine power has granted' everything needed for life and godliness, a benefactor's language. The proper response is grateful growth, not careless ingratitude.
37485: Jewish traditions about angels and judgment
37486: The angels who sinned are kept in 'Tartarus', a Greek word for the deepest underworld, echoing Jewish traditions about the Watchers found in 1 Enoch. 2 Peter tones down Jude's direct use of such traditions.
37488: In ancient historiography eyewitness testimony carried weight. The author contrasts 'cleverly devised myths' with what 'we were eyewitnesses' of on the holy mountain.
37489:
2 Peter stands firmly in Jewish apocalyptic and prophetic hope. It takes for granted that God judges the wicked and rescues the righteous, as with Noah, called a 'herald of righteousness', and Lot, who was distressed by Sodom's lawlessness. It relies on 'the prophetic word' as a lamp in a dark place until the day dawns. Its answer to the problem of delay draws on Psalm 90, 'a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday', a text Jewish interpreters also used when reflecting on God's timing.

The hope it defends is Isaiah's: 'new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells'. The Day of the Lord is the prophets' day of judgment and renewal, not a flight from creation. Its promise that believers may 'share in the divine nature' is expressed in Greek terms but, for a Jewish-rooted hearer, recalls Israel's calling to be holy as God is holy and the hope of escaping the corruption of the present age. For a first audience that had lived through Jerusalem's destruction and the deaths of the apostles, the message was that God keeps covenant promises, even when the wait is long.
37491: God's power and promises enable a growing life of virtue from faith to love.
37493: Facing death, Peter wants them to remember the truth after he is gone.
37495: The transfiguration and the prophets' Spirit-given word ground their hope.
37497: As in Israel's past, false teachers will come; God judged angels, the flood generation and Sodom.
37499: Scoffers forget creation and the flood; God's patience gives time to repent.
37501: Wait for new heavens and a new earth, live holy lives, and grow in grace.
37502: Remember and grow until the Day
37523: Personal, relational knowing of God and Jesus, the source of growth.
37525: Reverent devotion shown in a life that honours God.
37527: Royal arrival or presence; used of Christ's return.
37528: Long-suffering, slowness to anger, God's covenant character.
37529: Much of chapter 2 reworks Jude's examples and warnings, generally omitting Jude's explicit non-canonical sources.
37530: Refers to an earlier letter to the same readers.
37531: The transfiguration and the Lord coming like a thief echo the Gospels.
37532: Psalm 90 supplies the 'thousand years as one day' saying.
37533: The hope of new heavens and a new earth.
37534: Jesus is 'our God and Saviour', the beloved Son honoured on the holy mountain, and the coming Lord whose Day will bring judgment and renewal. Jewish readers recognise the Jewish testamentary form and apocalyptic hope; Christians read the letter as an assurance that Christ's promises remain sure across generations.
37535: The earth will be annihilated, so the physical world does not matter
37536: From the KJV ('the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up') many conclude God will destroy the physical universe and take believers to heaven, so caring for creation is pointless.
37537: The oldest Greek manuscripts read that the earth and its works 'will be found' (heurethesetai), meaning exposed or laid bare before God's judgment. Al Wolters, Richard Bauckham and J. Richard Middleton read the fire as refining and judging, like the flood, which did not annihilate the world but purged it. The goal is 'new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells', Isaiah's renewed creation.
37538: Some careful evangelical scholars (for example Thomas Schreiner and Douglas Moo) accept the 'found' reading, while noting that the language of dissolution is strong and that some discontinuity between present and future creation is intended. Others still hold a replacement view. The disagreement is about how much continuity there is, not about whether believers should be good stewards.
37539: If creation is destined for the trash heap, it can be neglected. If it is to be purified and renewed, present care for it anticipates God's future.
37540: 'A thousand years as one day' is a code for calculating prophecy
37541: Some read 2 Peter 3:8 as a formula: each day of creation equals a thousand years, so the world will last six thousand years and then Christ returns.
37542: The saying adapts Psalm 90:4 to make a point about God's perspective: human impatience cannot measure God's faithfulness, and his delay is patience. Bauckham and Gene Green read it as a pastoral answer to scoffers, not a timetable. Jesus himself says no one knows the day or hour.
37543: Some early Christian writers (for example the Epistle of Barnabas 15) did build a six-thousand-year scheme on such texts, and some modern readers find that tradition meaningful. Most evangelical scholars today agree the verse is not meant for date-setting.
37544: Date-setting repeatedly fails and discredits hope. The verse invites patience and repentance instead.
37545: For a church losing its founders and hearing mockery of its hope, 2 Peter said: remember the apostolic witness, grow in character, and understand God's delay as mercy.
